turns.prompt_text: I'm working in the fish terminal on a Mac. Specifically a Mac Mini.
turns.response_html:
Working with the fish (Friendly Interactive Shell) on a Mac Mini is a great choice—it offers excellent out-of-the-box features like autosuggestions and syntax highlighting that make terminal work feel much more modern than the default Zsh.

Since you're on macOS, here are a few tips to optimize your setup and some common commands to keep in your back pocket:

1. Essential Fish Commands

Fish handles things a bit differently than Bash or Zsh. Here are the "need-to-know" basics:

  • Configuring Fish: Instead of a .bashrc or .zshrc, Fish uses a config file located at ~/.config/fish/config.fish.
  • Setting Variables: To add a directory to your PATH (like for Homebrew or Mac-specific tools), use: set -Ua fish_user_paths /usr/local/bin (The -U makes it "Universal," meaning it persists across restarts).
  • Defining Aliases: You can create shortcuts easily: alias ll="ls -lah" Then save it permanently with funcsave ll.

2. Mac-Specific Integration

On a Mac Mini, you’ll likely want to ensure Homebrew is playing nice with Fish. If you haven't already, add this to your config.fish to make sure your Mac knows where your Brew-installed packages are:

if test -d /opt/homebrew/bin
    eval (/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv)
end

3. Boosting the Experience

Since you're already using a user-friendly shell, you might enjoy these "Quality of Life" tools that look great in a Mac terminal:

  • Fisher: A simple plugin manager for Fish.
  • Oh My Fish (OMF): Offers a huge library of themes.
  • Tide or Starship: Highly customizable prompts that show things like your current Git branch or Node version.

4. Useful Keybindings

  • → (Right Arrow): Accepts the grayed-out "autosuggestion" (one of Fish's best features).
  • Alt + →: Accepts only the next word of the suggestion.
  • Control + R: Searches through your command history.

turns.prompt_text: often I'm creating new functions. Or I'm asking an AI to build me a function. I would like to be able to copy the function that the AI gives me. And then when I go to the Fish terminal, run a command that takes what's in my clipboard and creates a new function
turns.response_html:
That is a classic Fish workflow improvement. Because Fish stores functions as individual .fish files in ~/.config/fish/functions/, you can actually automate this quite easily.

You can create a "meta-function" (a function that creates other functions) by reading the macOS clipboard using the pbpaste command.

The clipfunc Solution

Add this to your ~/.config/fish/config.fish file, or run it once and use funcsave clipfunc to keep it forever:

function clipfunc
    if test (count $argv) -eq 1
        set func_name $argv[1]
        set func_path ~/.config/fish/functions/$func_name.fish
        
        # Take clipboard content and wrap it if it doesn't have 'function' tags
        pbpaste > $func_path
        
        echo "Function '$func_name' created at $func_path"
        # Source it immediately so it's ready to use
        source $func_path
    else
        echo "Usage: clipfunc <function_name>"
    end
end

How to use it:

  1. Copy the code block the AI gives you.
  2. Go to your terminal and type: clipfunc my_new_command
  3. Run it: You can now immediately type my_new_command.

Pro-Tips for this Workflow:

  • Safety Check: If the AI gives you just the "body" of the code without the function name ... end wrapper, you’ll want to manually add those or I can help you update the script above to automatically wrap the clipboard text in those tags.
  • The funced Command: Fish has a built-in command called funced (function edit). If you already have a function and want to tweak it, just type funced -e nano function_name (or vim/code depending on your editor).
  • Persistence: By saving the file into ~/.config/fish/functions/, Fish will "lazy-load" it. It won't slow down your terminal startup, but it will be there the moment you call it.

turns.prompt_text: this is nice because I'm able to work a little simpler. Honestly, I would prefer to be able to just speech-to-text this as well. If I could just have an AI running in the terminal, that would really be nice. Because in essence, it really is just a translation layer for human-to-computer interaction.
turns.response_html:
That shift from "coding" to "translating intent" is exactly where the terminal is headed. Since you’re on a Mac Mini (likely Apple Silicon, which handles local AI beautifully), you have a few ways to turn your terminal into a voice-responsive assistant.

Given your fish setup and your interest in DIY electronics and automation, here are the best ways to bridge that human-to-computer gap:

1. The "Native" Assistant: tash (Terminal Assistant Shell)

There is a specific tool built for Fish users called tash. It acts as a middleware: if you type something Fish doesn't recognize (like "create a function to list all large files"), tash catches it, asks an AI, and drops the command directly into your command line for you to hit Enter.

  • Install: brew install renjfk/tap/tash
  • Why it fits: It’s lightweight and lives "at the heart" of your shell without replacing it.

2. The Local Voice Interface: VocaMac or agent-cli

If you want to literally speak to the terminal, you need a bridge that handles STT (Speech-to-Text) and then pipes that into a shell-aware AI.

  • VocaMac (Recommended for Mac): This is an open-source, 100% offline tool powered by WhisperKit. You hold a hotkey (like Right Option), speak your intent, and it types the text wherever your cursor is—including your Fish terminal.
    • The Workflow: You'd open your terminal, hold the key, say "write a fish function for X," and it appears instantly.
  • agent-cli: This is a more "power user" suite that includes Cmd+Shift+R to toggle voice transcription directly into the CLI. It uses Ollama locally, so your data stays on your Mac Mini.

3. The "Pure Translation" Layer: ask.sh

This tool is specifically designed to understand the context of your terminal (the last few lines of output, errors, etc.).

  • You run ask "why did that last command fail?" or ask "build me a function that does X".
  • It suggests the code and, with one keystroke, injects it into your prompt.

A "DIY" Speech-to-Function Bridge

Since you already have the clipfunc logic, you could combine it with a simple macOS "Dictation" workflow.

If you enable System Settings > Keyboard > Dictation, you can use a shortcut to speak directly into the terminal. If you say:

"function hello; echo 'hi'; end"

And then run your clipfunc (or a modified version that takes the last command), you've essentially built your own translation layer.
